2.text: younger brother with a stench!’ Then the old man and his wife went away. The whole time they

3.text: were weeping. Such was Tatk-omruˊwg̣ê, the violent, the richest reindeer-breeder on the whole

4.text: tundra. The Luck-giving Being (Kɪntaˊ-vaˊɪrg̣ɪn¹), in later time, however, made him poor.”²

5.text: Such a wandering life is still harder for women than for men; and those

6.text: of the “idle wanderers” who have wives cannot keep them for a long time,

7.text: unless the woman is also good for nothing, and undesirable for any other

8.text: man. Even then, in the middle of winter, the man takes care to leave the

9.text: woman, at least for a month or two, in the camp of some distant relative or

10.text: of a man who is of milder disposition and does not begrudge a morsel to a

11.text: wretched pauper. I remember one pair, — a man Ranaˊwkurg̣ɪn, and his

12.text: wife Añqaˊñña. Both were quite young. Ranaˊwkurg̣ɪn’s father died, and

13.text: left him, a young boy, with a large herd of reindeer. Before he was grown

14.text: up, half of the herd was gone. The other half he squandered away himself,

15.text: and lost the greater part of it through card-playing. Then he became quite

16.text: poor. At the time when I saw them they both had only one reindeer and

17.text: an old sledge. The woman was suffering, probably from syphilis; the man,

18.text: too, was lean and weak and good for nothing, as was plain at the first glance.

19.text: They even had no decent winter clothes, which is rarely the case even among

20.text: the “idle wanderers.” The necessity of warm clothing is so imperious, that

21.text: even the most careless fellows provide themselves with it in one way or an-

22.text: other. The woman tried once or twice to leave her husband for another man,

23.text: but nobody wanted her in his sleeping-room.

24.text: Another “idle-wanderer,” Yaqaˊq, was already an old man. His life was

25.text: much easier, because he had eight brothers, each with a “front house” in his

26.text: camp. He refused to have either tent or camp. He spent his time wandering

27.text: among the camps of his brothers; then he would move on and make visits

28.text: among the camps of the whole neighborhood. Because of his brothers he was

29.text: treated with consideration by the neighbors. Still another wanderer, ᴇndiˊw

30.text: by name, was of a very happy and serene disposition of mind. Even under

31.text: the most trying circumstances, he would only laugh and remain undisturbed.

32.text: Another man, Eleˊpqäi by name, wandered afoot among the camps, as much

33.text: in winter as in summer. His power of endurance was remarkable, even among

34.text: the Chukchee. In a most severe snow-storm he could sleep without a fire,

35.text: burrowing into a large bank of drifting snow. He staid without food for two

36.text: or three days almost as patiently as any wild animal. He spoke little. Upon

37.text: the whole, he seemed a specimen of some lower type of man.

38.text: The Neighboring Camp. — With the Reindeer Chukchee, who live in

39.text: small camps widely scattered over the tundra, the nearest camp forms the only

40.text: human group with whom one may have frequent intercourse. It is called

41.text: nɪm-takaˊčhɪn (“neighboring camp”). Nɪm is the root of the noun nɪˊmnɪm

43.text: ¹ The deity of reindeer-luck (cf. p. 314).
